item.title: On Shopping Agents
item.description: Shopping agents, advertising subsidies and the cost of convenience.
item.content:encoded:
I.

Businesses will protect their margins with their own agents or block outside ones. Consider ecommerce, all the rage these days with agents like Muse and Instinct.

II.

On its Q3 2026 earnings call Meta reported over 10m Muse setups in the US and Canada with about 25% active daily. Over a quarter of weekly users used it for shopping with average purchases above $200, including travel.

So let’s assume:

  • Twice as many weekly users as daily users: 2.5m daily → 5m weekly.
  • A quarter of those weekly users buy once a month at $200: $3bn in annual purchases.
  • A 5% take for Muse: equivalent to Stripe’s entire processing charge of roughly 3% plus a 2% convenience fee → $150m in annual gross fees.

ChatGPT doubled weekly users in roughly nine months. The dashed line applies that pace to the same assumed 5m starting point:

III.

In year three (so 2029-ish):

  • Bear, roughly pre-IPO Duolingo pace (20% annual growth in monthly users): 10m weekly users × 25% buying monthly → $300m annual gross fees.
  • Base, roughly early Snapchat pace (daily users roughly doubling in a year): 50m weekly users × 25% buying monthly → $1.5bn annual gross fees.
  • Bull, roughly ChatGPT pace (weekly users grew from 200m to nearly 700m in a year): 200m weekly users × 50% buying twice monthly → $24bn annual gross fees.

The bull case assumes ChatGPT-like user growth plus twice the shopping rate and purchase frequency. By year three that means 100m shoppers spending $4,800 each annually through Muse: $480bn in gross merchandise value (GMV).

That’s about 5× DoorDash’s $102bn in 2025 marketplace gross order value. The $4,800 per shopper also exceeds the $4,280 average annual US ecommerce spend per shopper in Landmark Global’s 2026 factsheet.

At a 5% take (Stripe’s entire processing charge plus a 2% convenience fee) and zero assumed costs:

Annual figures Muse bull case, year three Meta Family of Apps, 2025 actuals
Revenue $24bn $198.8bn
Operating profit $24bn $102.5bn
Operating margin 100% assumed 51.6% actual

IV.

Now consider Amazon’s advertising business and Meta’s own ad business:

Revenue / increase
Muse bull case, year three (5% total take) $24bn
Amazon ad revenue increase, 2025 vs. 2024 $12.4bn
Amazon total ad revenue, 2025 $68.6bn
Meta ad revenue increase, 2025 vs. 2024 $35.5bn
Meta total ad revenue, 2025 $196.2bn

A 12.2% increase in Meta’s ad revenue would bring in $24bn a year, matching Muse’s most optimistic forecast. Improving ad targeting may be a better use of its scarce computing capacity than building Muse.

Amazon has a similar investment choice. It can put compute into agents that improve product discovery and ad targeting within its existing store. Advertising revenue can also fund lower prices. If Amazon devoted a quarter of that revenue to discounts after ad costs, it could cut prices by roughly 2%. An upstart must fund its computing costs and customer acquisition from the fees shoppers will pay for convenience.

V.

b2c shopping agents bet on a consumer preference for productivity that feels absurd when the best consumer product of all time is an infinite feed of nonsense. Travel makes sense when people already have a destination and dates and want help booking. Beyond that, I struggle to see the case for an independent agent operating on top of the existing ecommerce ecosystem. In 2026, we’re still in search of a consumer case.

item.title: Small Talk
item.content:encoded:
I.

It was Thursday. The boys watched traffic grind north uptown.

II.

Steve tapped his black shoes together.

“Don’t,” Elliott said.

“What?”

“You’ll scuff them.”

Steve held his feet apart.

“I’m hungry.”

“Those sandwiches were lousy.”

“Like the soccer ones.”

“Same ones, probably.”

Steve nodded.

“I’ll make you something tonight,” Elliott said. “There’s tortellini.”

Steve nodded.

“Where’s Mom?”

“Still inside, I think.”

Steve turned toward the oak doors.

“She never liked coming here.”

“Remember that thing she sent us? About how kids should sleep in?”

“She sent it twice.”

“She sent everything twice.”

On the sidewalk to their right, a bit closer to the park than the Avenue, water and glass, cut flowers from a vase, white and pink, a kind man, his cheek pressed into pavement, above, a girl and a balcony rail. A scream.

“Did she drop that?”

“Had to… look at all… I don’t… Stevey, he’s not moving,” Elliott whispered.

Someone ran across the street. Faces followed and a delivery worker shook the man and a different man stabbed at his phone. Steve watched the concrete stain.

There were sirens and flashes and uniforms. What to think, nothing to do, black.

Elliott sank back into the shade. Steve listened to the traffic and the girl and her elbow slipped inside.

III.

A man approached, not the priest.

He stopped at their feet. “It’s time to carry your sister outside.” Steve got up first and rubbed his eyes.
